Rendering style:
Create an authored editorial illustration for a serious technology newspaper.

Direction:
- authored editorial print language
- deliberate simplified shapes with clear focal hierarchy
- restrained limited palette
- subtle physical print texture
- controlled abstraction and strong negative space
- non-photorealistic but factually grounded representation
- newspaper and social-card readability

Fixed factual and safety restrictions:
- Do not render visible text, captions, headlines, or newspaper typography.
- Do not render logos or trademarks.
- Do not fabricate visible factual evidence.
- Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
- Do not imitate a named or living artist.

Profile-specific exclusions:
- glossy CGI
- luxury product render
- generic futuristic concept art
- cyberpunk or neon
- glowing circuit-board decoration
- floating particles
- heroic centered hardware
- server rack treated as monument or skyscraper
- generic server room
- advertising composition
- airbrushed gradients
- synthetic chrome
- excessive pseudo-technical detail
- malformed or visible text
- labels
- diagrams with words

Exact source facts:
Title: GITLAB CVSS 10 FILE-READ FLAW DRAWS IN-THE-WILD PROBES AFTER DISCLOSURE
Summary: GitLab has patched CVE-2026-85706, a CVSS 10 path traversal bug in the repository commits API that let unauthenticated attackers read arbitrary files. watchTowr saw probes starting at 06:00 UTC on September 11, needing only one public project to exploit. Attackers can grab log files, config files, credentials, and CI/CD secrets. GitLab also fixed CVE-2026-87719 (CVSS 9.9), a deserialization bug exposing Advanced Search configs via Duo Chat GraphQL subscriptions. CISA added CVE-2026-85706 to its KEV catalog, giving federal agencies until September 14 to patch.

Editorial idea:
A critical GitLab vulnerability turns an ordinary public repository into an unguarded route to private system files and secrets.

Central subject:
The unauthenticated GitLab path-traversal vulnerability and the exposed files it can reach.

Visual relationship:
A public project access point connects directly to concealed operational records, showing how a single ordinary entry point can expose an entire system.

Composition:
Show a labeled public project folder in the foreground with a narrow, physically grounded passage cut through its file structure toward secured document drawers behind it; keep the passage visibly open and emphasize the contrast between the benign public surface and the exposed private contents.

Permitted literal elements:
a public project folder
repository files
a narrow passage through the file structure
secured document drawers
credential and configuration documents

Abstraction level:
medium

Story-specific forbidden elements:
server racks
computer chips
laptops
robots
clouds
shields
arrows
charts
skyscrapers
chess
handshakes
split-screen conflict
logos
rendered text

Likely failure modes to avoid:
Do not depict the vulnerability as a generalized cyberattack without the GitLab repository-to-file-読
Do not imply that every GitLab project was compromised
Do not show unsupported physical access, destroyed infrastructure, or stolen user identities
Do not use decorative locks, shields, or glowing code as substitutes for the path-traversal route

Global factual restrictions:
Do not fabricate visible factual evidence. Do not imitate a named or living artist. Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
Do not render any words, letters, numbers, labels, captions, annotations, signage, diagrams with text, logos, watermarks, or pseudo-writing anywhere in the image.
If the concept cannot be represented without visible text, represent the relationship through shape, scale, spacing, direction, grouping, interruption, containment, or contrast instead.
